To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the advantage of guidance begins when students are novices and continues as they acquire expertise, that this advantage is not due to a single factor but is due to the interaction of multiple factors, and that the advantage of guided instruction is most pronounced when the instructional task has a high cognitive load.

(a) minimally guided instruction does not work, and (b) the reason that it does not work is because it ignores both human cognitive architecture and empirical evidence from instructional studies over the past 40 years that consistently indicate that guidance during instruction is essential to effective and efficient learning.

1 ) unguided instruction and minimally guided instruction are less effective and less efﬁcient than guided instruction, 2 ) guided instruction is more efﬁcient and more effective for novices than for experts, 3 ) guidance is less effective for experts than it is for novices, and 4 ) guidance is more effective when it focuses on the acquisition and consolidation of declarative knowledge than when it focuses on procedural knowledge.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of instructional methods that maximize the efficiency and effectiveness of learning.
the question of how to improve instruction, not with whether to improve it.
how students learn and how this learning process can be facilitated by the design of effective instructional environments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
guided instruction is superior to unguided instruction.
the research evidence is overwhelmingly in favor of guidance during instruction, and that minimally guided or unguided instruction is inferior to guided instruction.
the failure of constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based teaching is a direct consequence of the lack of guidance provided during the learning process. [ 1 ]
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
guided instruction is more efficient than unguided or minimially guided instruction.

the most effective instructional methods are those that provide guidance during instruction, but that the guidance is provided in a manner consistent with what we now know about human cognitive architecture.
guidance is good, minimally guided instruction (or discovery learning) is bad, and direct instruction is better than discovery learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
instructional guidance is a critical element for effective instruction.
the effectiveness of instructional methods depends on how well these methods are matched with the characteristics of human cognitive architecture and the nature of the domain of instruction.
instructional design should be informed by our knowledge of human cognition, not by our beliefs about how people learn.
